analysis.one_liner: Lets the Consumer Product Safety Commission issue safety standards for guns and gun parts.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in a House subcommittee for the rest of the 118th Congress and died there.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law currently bans the Consumer Product Safety Commission from treating guns as consumer products, so the agency that sets safety rules for cribs, toys, and power tools has no authority over firearms. This bill strikes that exclusion, letting the commission write safety standards for pistols, revolvers, and other guns and their parts. It does not itself impose any rule; it restores the commission's authority to act. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and received no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people exposed to gun violence and accidental shootings, since safety standards could address defects like unsafe triggers or missing locking devices. Firearm buyers generally, who currently have no federal product-safety protections for guns.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun owners and households near gun violence

how_it_helps.text: Removes the 1970s-era exclusion of firearms from the Consumer Product Safety Act's definition of a consumer product, restoring the commission's authority to set safety standards for guns and firearm components.
The commission could issue mandatory safety standards for firearms, addressing hazards such as defective firing mechanisms, in the same way it regulates other consumer products.
The bill itself imposes no new rule; any standard would still go through the commission's normal public rulemaking process.

analysis.who_pays: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, who would face safety standards and compliance costs for the first time under consumer product law, and possibly dealers selling noncompliant products.

drawbacks.text: The Consumer Product Safety Commission has the power to ban products it finds too hazardous to sell, so gun-rights opponents argue that restoring its authority over firearms could amount to regulation by an unelected agency rather than by Congress, and raises Second Amendment concerns.

Compliance with new safety standards would raise manufacturing costs that could be passed to buyers, and the practical safety gains depend entirely on standards the commission chooses to write later, not on this bill's text.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives a safety agency authority it lacks over a product category linked to tens of thousands of American deaths a year, while costing gun makers compliance money and giving gun-rights advocates a real argument that the commission's ban authority could be used beyond narrow safety fixes. The safety case is real but indirect; nothing changes unless the commission actually writes standards, and any standard would face litigation and political pushback.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee, and the subcommittee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Robin Kelly introduced the Firearm Safety Act of 2023 on May 5, 2023, with 12 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, and on May 12, 2023, referred further to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever followed; the bill's action history ends with the subcommittee referral, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
Twenty-five House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers and gun dealers, who keep the decades-old exemption of guns from federal consumer product safety oversight, and officials who avoided a politically difficult vote on firearm regulation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers keeping their safety-rule exemption

for.name: Rep. Robin Kelly
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restore the Consumer Product Safety Commission's authority over firearms.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, controlled by Republicans in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction, sent it to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce, and never scheduled a markup or vote on it.

against.name: House Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after its May 12, 2023 referral with no hearing or action for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 25 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; with Republicans controlling the House and the Energy and Commerce Committee, the bill never advanced past a subcommittee referral.

industries.note: Guns have been exempt from Consumer Product Safety Act standards since the act's definition excluded them; this bill would make manufacturers subject to federal safety standards and product-liability-style oversight for the first time. Manufacturers have long opposed CPSC authority over firearms because the agency can also ban products it deems hazardous.

Dealers would face new compliance rules if the commission sets standards, but safer, defect-checked products could reduce liability exposure. Nothing changes unless the commission actually writes rules.
